facts.statement: Albertosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the latest Campanian to the early Maastrichtian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous, (latest Campanian–early Maastrichtian), ~(Possible earlier Campanian record)

facts.statement: Albertosaurus lived approximately 71 million years ago.
facts.quote: about 71 million years ago

facts.statement: Albertosaurus inhabited northwestern North America.
facts.quote: lived in northwestern North America

facts.statement: Albertosaurus grew up to 8 to 9 meters in length and weighed between 1.7 and 3.0 metric tons.
facts.quote: growing up to 8 - 9 m in length and weighing 1.7 - 3.0 MT

facts.statement: Albertosaurus was named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905.
facts.quote: named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in a one-page note at the end of his 1905 description of Tyrannosaurus

facts.statement: The genus name Albertosaurus refers to the Canadian province of Alberta, where the first remains were discovered in the same year the name was coined.
facts.quote: Its namesake is Alberta, the Canadian province established the very same year where the first remains were found

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Albertosaurus is Albertosaurus sarcophagus.
facts.quote: The type species is Albertosaurus sarcophagus

facts.statement: The type specimen of Albertosaurus is a partial skull collected on June 9, 1884.
facts.quote: The type specimen is a partial skull collected on June 9, 1884

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn assigned the name Albertosaurus sarcophagus to the Horseshoe Canyon skulls in 1905.
facts.quote: Osborn gave them the new name Albertosaurus sarcophagus in 1905

facts.statement: The holotype (CMN 5600) and paratype (CMN 5601) of Albertosaurus are housed in the Canadian Museum of Nature in Ottawa.
facts.quote: Both specimens, the holotype CMN 5600 and the paratype CMN 5601, are stored in the Canadian Museum of Nature in Ottawa

facts.statement: Barnum Brown discovered a large group of Albertosaurus fossils at a quarry near the Red Deer River on August 11, 1910.
facts.quote: On August 11, 1910, American paleontologist Barnum Brown discovered the remains of a large group of Albertosaurus at another quarry alongside the Red Deer River

facts.statement: Excavations at the Dry Island bonebed between 1997 and 2005 yielded remains of 13 additional Albertosaurus individuals.
facts.quote: Further excavation from 1997 to 2005 turned up the remains of 13 more individuals of various ages

facts.statement: A total of 1,128 Albertosaurus bones were recovered from the Dry Island bonebed, representing the largest known concentration of large theropod fossils from the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: A total of 1,128 Albertosaurus bones had been secured, which is the largest concentration of large theropod fossils known from the Cretaceous

facts.statement: William Parks described the species Albertosaurus arctunguis in 1928.
facts.quote: William Parks described a new species in 1928, Albertosaurus arctunguis

facts.statement: Since 1970, the species Albertosaurus arctunguis has been considered identical to Albertosaurus sarcophagus.
facts.quote: this species has been considered identical to A. sarcophagus since 1970

facts.statement: The specimen RTMP 81.010.001 was discovered in 1978 by amateur paleontologist Maurice Stefanuk.
facts.quote: Specimen RTMP 81.010.001 was found in 1978 by amateur paleontologist Maurice Stefanuk

facts.statement: The specimen RTMP 85.098.001 was found by Maurice Stefanuk on June 16, 1985.
facts.quote: RTMP 85.098.001 was found by Stefanuk on June 16, 1985

facts.statement: Indeterminate Albertosaurus fossils have been found in the Corral de Enmedio and Packard Formations of Mexico.
facts.quote: an indeterminate species ("cf. Albertosaurus sp.") has been discovered in the Corral de Enmedio and Packard Formations of Mexico

facts.statement: There is a scientific debate regarding the genus content of Albertosaurus, with some researchers recognizing Gorgosaurus libratus as a distinct species.
facts.quote: Scientists disagree on the content of the genus and some recognize Gorgosaurus libratus as a second species

facts.statement: Fossils reported from Montana, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Missouri are debated; they may not belong to Albertosaurus sarcophagus or the genus Albertosaurus at all.
facts.quote: Fossils have also been reported from the American states of Montana, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Missouri, but they are doubted to be from A. sarcophagus and may not even belong to the genus Albertosaurus

facts.statement: The discovery of 26 Albertosaurus individuals at a single site provides evidence of gregarious behavior.
facts.quote: The discovery of 26 individuals in one particular site provides evidence of gregarious behavior

facts.statement: The presence of an enlarged pneumatic opening in the palatine bone is considered a unique trait that validates Albertosaurus as a distinct taxon.
facts.quote: The possession of an enlarged pneumatic opening in the back rim of the side of the palatine bone proves that Albertosaurus is a valid taxon

facts.statement: Charles H. Sternberg recovered an Albertosaurus skeleton from the Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta in 1913.
facts.quote: In 1913, paleontologist Charles H. Sternberg recovered another tyrannosaurid skeleton from the slightly older Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta.

facts.statement: Lawrence Lambe originally named the species Gorgosaurus libratus in 1914.
facts.quote: Lawrence Lambe named this dinosaur Gorgosaurus libratus in 1914.

facts.statement: Dale Russell renamed Gorgosaurus libratus to Albertosaurus libratus in 1970, declaring Gorgosaurus a junior synonym of Albertosaurus.
facts.quote: Dale Russell declared the name Gorgosaurus a junior synonym of Albertosaurus, which had been named first, and G. libratus was renamed Albertosaurus libratus in 1970.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus specimens have been found in Alberta and Montana.
facts.quote: Other specimens were later found in Alberta and the US state of Montana.

facts.statement: Anatoly Nikolaevich Riabinin named Albertosaurus pericolosus in 1930 based on a Chinese tooth now thought to belong to Tarbosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1930, Anatoly Nikolaevich Riabinin named Albertosaurus pericolosus based on a tooth from China that probably belonged to Tarbosaurus.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul described Albertosaurus megagracilis in 1988 based on specimen LACM 28345 from the Hell Creek Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul based Albertosaurus megagracilis on a small tyrannosaurid skeleton, specimen LACM 28345, from the Hell Creek Formation of Montana.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul renamed Alectrosaurus olseni to Albertosaurus olseni in 1988, a classification that has not gained general acceptance.
facts.quote: In 1988, Paul renamed Alectrosaurus olseni (Gilmore 1933) into Albertosaurus olseni, but this has found no general acceptance.

facts.statement: Bryn Mader and Robert Bradley renamed Gorgosaurus novojilovi to Albertosaurus novojilovi in 1989.
facts.quote: In 1989, Gorgosaurus novojilovi (Maleev 1955) was renamed by Bryn Mader and Robert Bradley as Albertosaurus novojilovi.

facts.statement: William Diller Matthew renamed Albertosaurus sarcophagus to Deinodon sarcophagus in 1922.
facts.quote: In 1922, William Diller Matthew renamed A. sarcophagus into Deinodon sarcophagus.

facts.statement: Oskar Kuhn renamed Albertosaurus arctunguis to Deinodon arctunguis in 1939.
facts.quote: In 1939, German paleontologist Oskar Kuhn renamed A. arctunguis into Deinodon arctunguis.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus was a large bipedal predator, though smaller than Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus was a fairly large bipedal predator, but smaller than Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Typical adult Albertosaurus measured 8 to 9 meters long and weighed between 1.7 and 3.0 metric tons.
facts.quote: Typical Albertosaurus adults measured up to 8 - 9 m long and weighed between 1.7 and 3.0 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus had long legs ending in a four-toed foot with a very short hallux that did not touch the ground.
facts.quote: The legs were long and ended in a four-toed foot on which the first toe, the hallux, was very short and did not reach the ground.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus may have been capable of walking speeds between 14 and 21 kilometers per hour.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus may have been able to reach walking speeds of 14–21 km/hour (8–13 mi/hour).

facts.statement: Two skin impressions of Albertosaurus are known, both showing scales.
facts.quote: Two skin impressions from Albertosaurus are known, and both show scales.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus belly scales were pebbly and gradually became larger and somewhat hexagonal in shape.
facts.quote: The scales are pebbly and gradually become larger and somewhat hexagonal in shape.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus is one of only two known theropods with preserved feature scales, which were placed 4.5 centimeters apart.
facts.quote: Also preserved are two larger feature scales, placed 4.5 centimeters apart from each other, making Albertosaurus, along with Carnotaurus, the only known theropods with preserved feature scales.

facts.statement: Another Albertosaurus skin impression shows small, diamond-shaped scales arranged in rows.
facts.quote: These scales are small, diamond-shaped, and arranged in rows.

facts.statement: The largest adult Albertosaurus had a massive skull about 1 meter long perched on a short, S-shaped neck.
facts.quote: The massive skull of Albertosaurus, which was perched on a muscular, short, S-shaped neck, was about 1 m long in the largest adults.

facts.statement: The jaws of Albertosaurus contained 58 or more banana-shaped teeth in total.
facts.quote: Its long jaws contained, both sides combined, 58 or more banana-shaped teeth.

facts.statement: The four premaxillary teeth at the tip of each upper jaw were smaller, closely packed, and D-shaped in cross-section.
facts.quote: The premaxillary teeth at the tip of the upper jaw, four per side, were much smaller than the rest, more closely packed, and D-shaped in cross section.

facts.statement: The maximum bite force of Albertosaurus, measured at the back teeth, reached 3,413 Newtons.
facts.quote: The bite force of Albertosaurus was less formidable, however, with the maximum force, by the back teeth, reaching 3,413 Newtons.

facts.statement: Short bony crests above the eyes of Albertosaurus may have been brightly colored and used by males for courtship.
facts.quote: Above the eyes were short bony crests that may have been brightly coloured in life and possibly used, by males in particular, in courtship to attract a mate.

facts.statement: William Abler demonstrated that teeth with ampullas are structurally stronger, similar to how drilled holes make plexiglass 25% stronger than bars with only regular incisions.
facts.quote: Abler demonstrated that a plexiglass bar with incisions called "kerfs" and drilled holes was more than 25% stronger than one with only regularly placed incisions.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus belongs to the theropod family Tyrannosauridae and the subfamily Albertosaurinae.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus is a member of the theropod family Tyrannosauridae, specifically the subfamily Albertosaurinae.

facts.statement: The closest relative of Albertosaurus is the slightly older Gorgosaurus libratus.
facts.quote: Its closest relative is the slightly older Gorgosaurus libratus (sometimes called Albertosaurus libratus; see below).

facts.statement: Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus are the only described species in the subfamily Albertosaurinae, though other undescribed species may exist.
facts.quote: These two species are the only described albertosaurines, but other undescribed species may exist.

facts.statement: There is a debate among authors regarding whether Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus should remain separate genera, with most following Philip J. Currie's recommendation to keep them separate but some disagreeing.
facts.quote: Most authors have followed Currie's recommendation, but some have not.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Albertosaurus sternbergi is a juvenile Gorgosaurus libratus, identical to Tyrannosaurus, or a separate genus named Nanotyrannus.
facts.quote: The former species is today seen as a juvenile form of Gorgosaurus libratus and the latter is seen as either identical to Tyrannosaurus or representing a separate genus, Nanotyrannus.

facts.statement: The classification of Alectrosaurus olseni as Albertosaurus olseni proposed in 1988 has not found general acceptance.
facts.quote: In 1988, Paul renamed Alectrosaurus olseni (Gilmore 1933) into Albertosaurus olseni, but this has found no general acceptance.

facts.statement: The youngest known Albertosaurus was a two-year-old individual weighing approximately 50 kilograms and measuring slightly more than 2 meters in length.
facts.quote: The youngest known Albertosaurus is a two-year-old discovered in the Dry Island bonebed, which would have weighed about 50 kilograms (110 lb) and measured slightly more than 2 m long.

facts.statement: The oldest and largest known Albertosaurus specimen was 28 years old and measured 10 meters in length.
facts.quote: The 10 m specimen from the same quarry is 28 years old, the oldest and largest one known.

facts.statement: Based on an adult weight of 1.3 tonnes, the rapid growth phase of Albertosaurus occurred at a rate of 122 kilograms per year.
facts.quote: The growth rate during this phase was 122 kg per year, based on an adult weighing 1.3 tonnes.

facts.statement: The end of the rapid growth phase in Albertosaurus suggests the onset of sexual maturity, though growth continued at a slower rate for the rest of their lives.
facts.quote: The end of the rapid growth phase suggests the onset of sexual maturity in Albertosaurus, although growth continued at a slower rate throughout the animals' lives.

facts.statement: Most known Albertosaurus individuals were 14 years old or older when they died.
facts.quote: Most known Albertosaurus individuals were aged 14 years or older at the time of death.

facts.statement: Mortality rates in Albertosaurus doubled at age twelve and again between ages fourteen and sixteen, coinciding with rapid growth and sexual maturity.
facts.quote: Mortality rates doubled at age twelve, perhaps the result of the physiological demands of the rapid growth phase, and then doubled again with the onset of sexual maturity between the ages of fourteen and sixteen.

facts.statement: The Dry Island bonebed, discovered by Barnum Brown, contains the remains of 26 Albertosaurus, the highest number of individuals found in one locality for any large Cretaceous theropod.
facts.quote: The Dry Island bonebed discovered by Barnum Brown and his crew contains the remains of 26 Albertosaurus, the most individuals found in one locality of any large Cretaceous theropod and the second-most of any large theropod dinosaur behind the Allosaurus assemblage at the Cleveland-Lloyd Dinosaur Quarry in Utah.

facts.statement: The Dry Island bonebed group included one very old adult, eight adults aged 17 to 23, seven sub-adults aged 12 to 16, and six juveniles aged 2 to 11.
facts.quote: The group seems to be composed of one very old adult, eight adults between 17 and 23 years old, seven sub-adults undergoing their rapid growth phases at between 12 and 16 years old, and six juveniles between the ages of 2 and 11 years old that had not yet reached the growth phase.

facts.statement: Some scientists debate whether the Dry Island bonebed represents pack behavior or if the animals were driven together by environmental factors like drought or flood.
facts.quote: Other scientists are skeptical, observing that the animals may have been driven together by a drought, flood, or other reasons.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Albertosaurus social behavior involved pack hunting or mobbing carcasses, where competition led to killing and cannibalism.
facts.quote: Others have speculated that, instead of social groups, at least some of these finds represent Komodo dragon-like mobbing of carcasses, where aggressive competition leads to some of the predators being killed and even cannibalized.

facts.statement: Evidence of cannibalism in Albertosaurus was reported in 2024 by Coppock and Currie.
facts.quote: The evidence of cannibalism was later reported in 2024 by Coppock and Currie.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown's colleague Currie hypothesized that younger Albertosaurus drove prey toward larger, slower adults in a pack-hunting strategy.
facts.quote: Currie hypothesized that the younger members of the pack may have been responsible for driving their prey towards the adults, who were larger and more powerful, but also slower.

facts.statement: In 2010, Currie admitted that while he favored the pack-hunting hypothesis, the Dry Island concentration could have been caused by a slowly rising water level during a flood.
facts.quote: In 2010, Currie, though still favouring the hunting pack hypothesis, admitted that the concentration could have been brought about by other causes, such as a slowly rising water level during an extended flood.

facts.statement: In 2009, researchers hypothesized that smooth-edged holes in Albertosaurus fossil jaws were caused by a bird-like parasite.
facts.quote: In 2009, researchers hypothesized that smooth-edged holes found in the fossil jaws of tyrannosaurid dinosaurs, such as Albertosaurus, were caused by a parasite similar to Trichomonas gallinae, which infects birds.

facts.statement: A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild found stress fractures in only one of 319 checked Albertosaurus foot bones and none in four hand bones.
facts.quote: In 2001, Bruce Rothschild and others published a study examining evidence for stress fractures and tendon avulsions in theropod dinosaurs and the implications for their behavior. They found that only one of the 319 Albertosaurus foot bones checked for stress fractures actually had them and none of the four hand bones did.

facts.statement: In 1970, Dale Russel reported pathological damage to the humeri of two of five Albertosaurus sarcophagus specimens.
facts.quote: In 1970, two of the five Albertosaurus sarcophagus specimens with humeri were reported by Dale Russel as having pathological damage to them.

facts.statement: Three foot phalanges of a Dry Island Albertosaurus assembly show enthesophytes, but their cause remains unknown.
facts.quote: On three phalanges of the foot, strange bony spurs that consisted of abnormal ossifications of the tendons, so-called enthesophytes, were present, but their cause is unknown.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Dry Island assembly show broken and healed ribs, a puncture wound on a jaw, and healed and unhealed bite marks.
facts.quote: Two ribs and a belly-rib showed signs of breaking and healing. One adult specimen had a left lower jaw showing a puncture wound and both healed and unhealed bite marks.

facts.statement: Most Albertosaurus sarcophagus fossils come from the upper Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, dating to the early Maastrichtian (70 to 68 million years ago).
facts.quote: Most fossils of Albertosaurus sarcophagus are known from the upper Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta. These younger units of this geologic formation date to the early Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, about 70 to 68 million years ago.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus remains are found in delta and floodplain deposits from the later half of the Horseshoe Canyon times.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus remains are found in deposits laid down in the deltas and floodplains of large rivers during the later half of Horseshoe Canyon times.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus sarcophagus has synonyms including Deinodon sarcophagus (Osborn, 1905) and Albertosaurus arctunguis (Parks, 1928).
facts.quote: synonyms: Deinodon sarcophagus (Osborn, 1905) Albertosaurus arctunguis Parks, 1928 Deinodon arctunguis (Parks, 1928)

facts.statement: Albertosaurus sarcophagus lived in western North America during the late Cretaceous, between 71 and 68 million years ago.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus sarcophagus (gr., «lagarto de Alberta comedor de carne») es la única especie conocida del género extinto Albertosaurus de dinosaurio terópodo tiranosáurido que vivió en el oeste de América del Norte a finales del período Cretácico, entre 71 y 68 millones de años, a comienzos del Maastrichtiense.

facts.statement: There is scientific disagreement regarding whether the genus Albertosaurus represents one or two species.
facts.quote: Existe cierto desacuerdo en la comunidad científica en cuanto al número de especies representadas en el género, que según el caso serían una o dos.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus was a bipedal predator with a large head, jaws with dozens of large teeth, and small two-fingered hands.
facts.quote: Al ser un tiranosáurido, los albertosaurios fueron depredadores bípedos con una gran cabeza, mandíbulas provistas de docenas de grandes dientes y pequeñas «manos» de dos dedos.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus was likely as heavy as a modern black rhinoceros, much smaller than its relative Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Aunque sea relativamente grande para un terópodo, Albertosaurus era mucho más pequeño que su famoso pariente Tyrannosaurus, probablemente pesando tanto como un rinoceronte negro moderno.

facts.statement: Fossils of more than thirty individuals have been discovered, providing detailed anatomical knowledge of Albertosaurus.
facts.quote: Han sido descubiertos fósiles de más de treinta individuos, permitiendo a los científicos un conocimiento más detallado de la anatomía de Albertosaurus que la que se tiene de otros tiranosáuridos.

facts.statement: The discovery of twenty-six individuals together at one site suggests group behavior and allows developmental biology studies.
facts.quote: El hallazgo de veintiséis individuos juntos en un sitio señala evidencia de comportamiento en grupos y permite estudios de su biología del desarrollo, imposibles con animales menos conocidos.

facts.statement: Adult Albertosaurus reached approximately nine meters in length, with some older individuals reaching ten meters.
facts.quote: Los adultos alcanzaban aproximadamente nueve metros de largo, mientras que algunos individuos, los de mayor edad, habrían alcanzado los diez metros.

facts.statement: Independent estimates suggest an adult Albertosaurus weighed between 1.3 and 1.7 tons, with a maximum of 2.5 tons.
facts.quote: Varias estimaciones independientes sobre su masa, obtenidas mediante diferentes métodos, sugieren que un Albertosaurus adulto habría pesado entre 1,3 y 1,7 y un máximo de 2,5 toneladas.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus was bipedal and balanced its heavy head and torso with a long tail.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus era bípedo y balanceaba su pesada cabeza y tronco con una larga cola.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus had extremely small forelimbs with only two fingers relative to its body size.
facts.quote: Los miembros delanteros de los tiranosáuridos eran extremadamente pequeños para su tamaño y tenían solamente dos dedos.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus had long hind limbs ending in a four-toed foot, with the first toe small and posterior, and the middle toe longer than the others.
facts.quote: Los miembros traseros eran largos y terminaban en un pie de cuatro dedos. El primero de estos dedos era muy pequeño y se ubicaba en la parte posterior, y solo los otros tres se apoyaban en el suelo, con el dedo medio más largo que los demás.

facts.statement: The largest adult Albertosaurus skulls were approximately one meter long.
facts.quote: El enorme cráneo de Albertosaurus, sostenido por un cuello corto con forma de S, medía aproximadamente un metro de largo en los adultos más grandes.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus possessed more than sixty slightly curved teeth, a higher count than larger tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Sus largas mandíbulas contenían más de sesenta dientes ligeramente curvados, muchos en comparación con los tiranosáuridos más grandes, que poseían menos dientes.

facts.statement: The premaxillary teeth at the front of the upper jaw were much smaller, compact, and D-shaped in cross-section.
facts.quote: Los dientes premaxilares, en el extremo del maxilar superior, eran mucho más pequeños que el resto, compactos y con sección en forma de D.

facts.statement: The maximum bite force exerted by the posterior teeth of Albertosaurus reached 3413 newtons.
facts.quote: La fuerza máxima ejercida por los dientes posteriores llegaba a 3413 newton.

facts.statement: In 2001, William Abler observed that the striations on Albertosaurus teeth are so fine they can functionally be considered a crack in the tooth.
facts.quote: William Abler observó en 2001 que las estrías de los dientes de Albertosaurus son tan finas que pueden ser funcionalmente una grieta en el diente.

facts.statement: Similar fractures found in ancient predators like phytosaurs and Dimetrodon lacked adaptations to prevent crack propagation, unlike those in tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: En un examen de otros depredadores antiguos, como un fitosaurio y en Dimetrodon, se han encontrado de manera similar fracturas como estrías, pero no adaptaciones para la prevención de la propagación de grietas.

facts.statement: Wear patterns on the teeth suggest that head-shaking behavior may have been involved in tyrannosaurid feeding.
facts.quote: Los patrones de desgaste de los dientes insinúan que el comportamiento de sacudir la cabeza puede haber estado involucrado en la alimentación de los tiranosáuridos.

facts.statement: The first Albertosaurus was found by Joseph Burr Tyrrell during geological prospecting in 1884.
facts.quote: El primer Albertosaurus fue encontrado por Joseph Burr Tyrrell durante unas prospecciones geológicas en 1884.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus was named in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn of the American Museum of Natural History in a brief note at the end of his description of Tyrannosaurus rex.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus fue nombrado en 1905 por Henry Fairfield Osborn, del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, en una muy breve nota al final de su descripción de Tyrannosaurus rex.

facts.statement: The name honors Alberta, the Canadian province where the first remains were found.
facts.quote: El nombre hace honor a Alberta, la provincia canadiense en la cual se encontraron los primeros restos.

facts.statement: More than thirty specimens of various ages are known.
facts.quote: Se conocen más de treinta especímenes de diversas edades.

facts.statement: The type specimen was found on June 9, 1884, and recovered by an expedition of the Geological Survey of Canada led by geologist Joseph Burr Tyrrell.
facts.quote: Este espécimen, encontrado el 9 de junio de 1884, fue recuperado por una expedición del Instituto Geológico de Canadá, dirigido por el famoso geólogo Joseph Burr Tyrrell.

facts.statement: In 1889, Thomas Chesmer Weston, a colleague of Tyrrell, found an additional smaller incomplete skull and some additional skeletal material at a nearby location.
facts.quote: En 1889, el colega de Tyrell Thomas Chesmer Weston encontró un cráneo incompleto adicional más pequeño y algo más de material esquelético en una localización cercana.

facts.statement: The two skulls were assigned to the species Laelaps incrassatus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1892.
facts.quote: Los dos cráneos fueron asignados a la especie Laelaps incrassatus por Edward Drinker Cope en 1892.

facts.statement: Because D. incrassatus was based only on generic tyrannosaurid teeth, Osborn created the new name Albertosaurus sarcophagus in 1905 for the distinct Horseshoe Canyon skulls.
facts.quote: Finalmente, puesto que el D. incrassatus se basaba solamente en dientes genéricos de tiranosáurido que no podían indicar fácilmente su asignación a una especie en particular. Los cráneos del cañón Horseshoe difieren notablemente de los restos de Dryptosaurus aquilunguis, tipo nomenclatural del Dryptosaurus, por lo que Osborn creó el nuevo nombre Albertosaurus sarcophagus para ellos en 1905.

facts.statement: In 2010, Thomas Carr established that the holotype, paratype, and comparable specimens shared a unique autapomorphy, proving Albertosaurus is a valid taxon.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, en 2010 Thomas Carr estableció que el holotipo, el paratipo y los posteriores ejemplares comparables encontrados compartían un rasgo común único o autapomorfía, la posesión de una abertura neumática amplia en el borde posterior de un lado del hueso palatino, lo que demuestra que Albertosaurus era un taxón válido.

facts.statement: Albertosaurus belongs to the parent group Albertosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Albertosaurinae

facts.statement: Albertosaurus is classified in the family Tyrannosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Tyrannosauridae

facts.statement: Albertosaurus lived from the Santonian to the Maastrichtian, between 85.7 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Santonian to Maastrichtian (85.7 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Williams et al. (2026) presented evidence of preserved micro- and nanoscale histological features in bones of Albertosaurus sarcophagus from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: Evidence of preservation of micro- and nanoscale histological features (including Haversian canal and lacunocanalicular network permineralization) in bones of Albertosaurus sarcophagus from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation (Alberta, Canada) is presented by Williams et al. (2026).

rejected.quote: bipedal predator with short arms, two-fingered hands, and a massive head with dozens of large, sharp teeth
